reading.body:
AI operations face business interruption risk from at least ten distinct failure modes spanning power, compute, and connectivity, with power grid issues forming the largest cluster.

Four of the ten listed exposures concern electricity supply or grid connection: utility load shedding, power purchase agreement failure, interconnection queue delay, and drought-related water shutoffs. This concentration reflects the grid's role as the binding constraint on AI scaling, where a stoppage in megawatts or cooling water halts compute regardless of how many GPUs are installed.

The remaining exposures show that interruption risk follows the AI stack outward, from GPU provider service level breaches and foundational API outages to hyperscaler cascades, subsea fibre cuts, edge node corruption, and dark fibre disruption. Each point names a specific coverage product, which means insurers have begun to underwrite these AI-specific failure modes rather than treating them as generic business interruption.

The data does not state premiums, limits, claim frequency, or which exposures cause the largest losses. It also does not indicate how these coverages interact or whether any single policy bundles multiple failure modes.

The ten exposures split into two groups that fail on different clocks. Power and grid items, four of the ten, fail slowly and predictably: interconnection queue delay is measured in years, drought in seasons, load shedding in peak hours. Connectivity and software items, the other six, fail in seconds to hours. A reader insuring an AI operator is buying two different products, one for a slow squeeze and one for a sudden stop.

The list also separates failures by who is contractually upstream. Power purchase agreement failure and GPU provider service level breaches are counterparty failures, where a named party owes performance. Utility load shedding, drought shutoffs, subsea cuts, and dark fibre disruption are not: no one promised the megawatts or the route. Contingent business interruption, hyperscaler cascades, and foundational API outages sit in between, because the loss arrives through a third party the insured never contracted with.

The practical consequence is that a single AI site can be hit by several of these at once and the list gives no way to tell which coverage responds first. A drought shutoff that forces a site offline is simultaneously a water event, a power event, and a business interruption event. Nothing in the data says whether these are written as separate policies, sublimits, or exclusions of one another.

What counts as a power grid exposure on this list?
Four of the ten points concern electricity or cooling supply: utility load shedding and throttling, power purchase agreement failure, interconnection queue delay, and drought-related water shutoffs.

Which exposures involve a third party that never contracted with the insured?
Utility load shedding, drought-related water shutoffs, subsea fibre cuts, and dark fibre backhaul disruption all describe losses from parties outside the insured's contracts. Hyperscaler cascades and foundational API outages also arrive through third parties, though the insured typically has a service relationship with the cloud or model provider.

Does the data say how much any of these stoppages costs?
No. The data names coverage products and failure modes but contains no premiums, limits, loss amounts, or claim frequency.

Are these ten coverages sold separately or bundled?
The data does not say. Each point names a distinct coverage product, and nothing indicates whether a single policy combines them or whether they exclude one another.

Which exposure is most likely to hit first for a new AI site?
The data does not rank likelihood. Interconnection queue delay is the only item described as slipping by years, while load shedding, cable cuts, and API outages are described as events rather than schedules.

Why does the list include water when the subject is power?
Drought-related water shutoffs appear because cooling water is a grid-adjacent dependency: a municipality cutting water halts compute the same way a utility cutting megawatts does. The data groups it with the power items rather than with the connectivity ones.
